title: The imperfect and the augment

objectives.can: Recognise an imperfect indicative by its augment and endings and parse it.

explanation.summary: The imperfect is the past tense-form of the present stem. It is marked by an augment at the front of the verb and by endings that differ a little from the present's. Like the present, it usually views an action as in progress, repeated or habitual, but now in the past.

sections.heading: Present stem, past time
body: The imperfect is built on the same stem as the present: λεγ- gives λέγω and ἔλεγον, ἐρχ- gives ἔρχομαι and ἤρχετο. What changes is the augment and the endings. In the indicative the imperfect usually places an action in the past, and, like the present, it usually views the action as going on, repeated, or habitual rather than as a single whole.

A good English translation is often 'was saying', 'used to say' or 'kept saying', but the Greek form means none of these by itself. In narrative, the imperfect is often used for the setting and for background: what was going on, what people were doing, what a person's habit was. Do not translate it mechanically: look at the sentence.

sections.heading: The augment
body: The augment is the sign of past time in the indicative. It takes three forms, depending on the first letter of the verb.

A verb that begins with a consonant takes a syllabic augment, a short ἐ- placed in front: λέγω gives ἔλεγον, and κράζω gives ἔκραζον. A verb that begins with a vowel takes a temporal augment, which lengthens the vowel: α and ε become η (ἀκούω gives ἤκουον, ἀγαπάω gives ἠγάπα, ἐσθίω gives ἤσθιον, ἔρχομαι gives ἤρχετο) and ο becomes ω (ὀφείλω gives ὤφειλεν). A vowel that is already long (η or ω) is left alone. Diphthongs and a few other vowels change in their own ways, and the lexicon will show them.

In a compound verb the augment goes between the prefix and the stem, not at the front of the word: ἐκπορεύομαι gives ἐξεπορεύετο, and διαμερίζω gives διεμέριζον. The prefix may lose or change its last vowel before the augment (δια- becomes δι-).

sections.heading: The endings
body: The imperfect uses the 'secondary' endings, the set that goes with past tenses. The active has the connecting vowel ο/ε as in the present and the endings -ον, -ες, -ε(ν), -ομεν, -ετε, -ον. The middle and passive have -όμην, -ου, -ετο, -όμεθα, -εσθε, -οντο, which replace the present's -ομαι, -ῃ, -εται, -ονται and the rest.
Note that the first person singular and third person plural of the active are the same form: ἔλεγον can mean 'I was saying' or 'they were saying'. The context shows which.

sections.heading: Contract verbs and εἰμί
body: Contract verbs take the augment and then contract: ποιέω gives ἐποίει (singular) and ἐποίουν (plural), ἀγαπάω gives ἠγάπα, ζητέω gives ἐζήτουν, πληρόω gives ἐπλήρου. The contraction rules of the second lesson of this unit apply unchanged.

εἰμί, 'I am', has an irregular imperfect: ἦν, ἦσαν and the rest. ἦν is one of the commonest words in the New Testament, with several hundred occurrences. It is used for the setting and for descriptions.

sections.heading: How to recognise an imperfect
body: Look at the beginning and the end. An ἐ- or a lengthened vowel at the front, and -ον, -ες, -ε(ν), -ετο or -οντο at the end, is an imperfect or an aorist. The two tenses use the same augment and nearly the same endings, so the stem decides: ἔλεγον and ἤρχετο are imperfects because they use the present stem; εἶπον and ἦλθον are aorists because they use a different stem. Aorists are taught in the next unit.

misunderstandings: The augment is not part of the stem. When you look a verb up in the lexicon, take the augment off first: ἤκουον is under ἀκούω, ἠγάπα under ἀγαπάω.
The augment is found only in the indicative. Participles, infinitives, subjunctives and imperatives of the same tense-form have no augment.

The imperfect is not just 'a longer past'. It is the past tense-form that views an action as in progress, repeated or habitual. A single completed event is more often put in the aorist, which you will meet next.
ἔλεγον does not always mean 'I was saying'. It can be the first person singular or the third person plural ('they were saying'), and in the Gospels it is very often the plural.

deeper.heading: ἔχω and the other irregular augments
body: A few verbs do not follow the rules above. The imperfect of ἔχω is εἶχον, with a diphthong, where the rule you have just learned would lead you to expect a plain lengthened vowel; and θέλω has the imperfect ἤθελον, as if the verb began with a vowel.  These forms are best learned as they come, from the reading and the lexicon.

examples.analysis: ἐξεπορεύετο (singular) and ἐβαπτίζοντο (plural) are third person imperfects. The first is middle in form with an active sense, from ἐκπορεύομαι: the augment stands between the prefix ἐκ (ἐξ) and the stem. ἐβαπτίζοντο is passive, with the agent given by ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ, and begins with a syllabic augment ἐ-. The scene is repeated or ongoing: people kept coming and kept being baptised.

The imperfect paints the scene: the disciples were plucking and eating while they walked.
